subject: Climate & Environment
title: Air Quality Monitoring
description: A quick, practical guide to Air Quality Monitoring.

hook.text: You can check the air quality of any city in the world from your phone, right now.

buildup.text: Government monitoring stations measure PM2.5, ozone, NO₂, and SO₂ around the clock.

discovery.text: Low-cost sensors now let communities build their own monitoring networks for under $200.

twist.text: In some countries, official data is suppressed. Citizen networks fill the gap.

climax.text: Real-time data lets people avoid polluted routes, times, and areas to reduce exposure.

punchline.text: You can't fix what you can't measure. Now anyone can measure.

quiz.question: How have low-cost sensors changed air quality monitoring?
options: Communities can build their own monitoring networks

details.summary: Air quality monitoring uses ground-based stations, satellite sensors, and low-cost portable devices to measure pollutant concentrations in real time. This data underpins health advisories, regulatory enforcement, and scientific research on pollution trends.
details.whyItMatters: You cannot manage what you cannot measure. Monitoring networks reveal pollution hotspots, track policy effectiveness, and power apps that help individuals reduce exposure.
takeaways: Reference-grade stations cost hundreds of thousands of dollars each
Low-cost sensors are expanding coverage in underserved areas
Satellite data fills gaps where no ground monitors exist

faq.question: What does the Air Quality Index number actually mean?
faq.answer: The AQI converts pollutant concentrations into a scale from 0 to 500. Values under 50 are good, 51 to 100 are moderate, and above 150 is unhealthy for everyone. Different countries use slightly different scales and breakpoints.

faq.question: How accurate are low-cost air quality sensors?
faq.answer: Low-cost sensors can track pollution trends but may drift over time and are sensitive to humidity. Calibrating them against reference monitors improves accuracy. They are best used to complement, not replace, regulatory-grade stations.
